2. OIDC Federation: No Long-Lived Secrets
OIDC federation lets GitHub Actions genuinely assume a real AWS IAM role directly, with no long-lived, real secret stored in GitHub at all.
This directly applies the temporary-credentials preference already covered in IAM Best Practices, GitHub Actions is precisely where this genuinely matters most.
This is the real, modern, preferred approach, considerably safer than storing a real, static AWS access key as a GitHub secret.
Setting this up takes real, one-time configuration, both in AWS IAM and in the workflow itself, worth the genuine, upfront investment.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784573488503-612451412.png
blocks.alt: No long-lived, real secret stored anywhere, genuinely safer than a static access key

permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read

jobs:
  terraform:
    steps:
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/github-actions-terraform
          aws-region: us-east-1

blocks.content: 3. Recap: The fmt, validate, plan Order
blocks.text: 3. Recap: The fmt, validate, plan Order

blocks.content: Recall the real, deliberate CI pipeline order already covered in Code Validation, fmt, then validate, then plan, cheapest and fastest checks running first.
This exact, real order is what this GitHub Actions workflow follows directly, each step only genuinely running if the previous one actually succeeds.
This connects directly back to that earlier, already-covered guidance, now delivered as a real, concrete, working GitHub Actions workflow.
Following this order consistently saves real, genuine CI time, and surfaces problems at the earliest, cheapest, real possible stage.
Each step's genuine failure stops the entire, real job immediately, exactly the fail-fast behavior this deliberate ordering is actually built around.

blocks.alt: The real order already covered, now the actual, working order of this workflow

  terraform:
    steps:

blocks.content: 4. Workflow Triggers
A real workflow trigger, push or pull_request, determines exactly when this entire, real pipeline actually starts running at all.
Triggering on pull_request lets a real plan run automatically for review, covered further in the Plan Stage topic ahead, before anything real merges.
Triggering on push to a real, trusted branch, main, typically, is what triggers the real apply stage, covered in its own, dedicated topic ahead.
Choosing these triggers deliberately is what actually connects a real, live GitHub repository to this entire, automated Terraform pipeline.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784573492319-899876423.png
blocks.alt: Real events, genuinely starting this entire pipeline, at exactly the right, deliberate moment

blocks.content:
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  push:
    branches: [main]

blocks.content: 6. A Real, Complete Example
Bringing this topic together, a real, complete GitHub Actions workflow combines OIDC federation, the fmt-validate-plan order, and real, deliberate triggers.
This is worth treating as a genuine, real starting template, ready to actually run against a real, live repository with minimal, real adaptation.
Every practice covered in this topic individually comes together here, into one, coherent, real, working CI pipeline.
This exact foundation is what the Plan Stage and Apply Stage topics ahead build genuinely deeper, real, practical detail on top of.

name: Terraform
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read

jobs:
  terraform:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/github-actions-terraform
          aws-region: us-east-1
      - run: terraform init
      - run: terraform fmt -check -recursive
      - run: terraform validate
      - run: terraform plan

blocks.content: A real matrix strategy runs the exact same, real pipeline once per real, separate environment, dev, staging, production, without genuinely duplicating any workflow code.
This connects directly to Environment Separation, the closing topic of this module, covered there in full, dedicated, practical depth.
This is worth introducing briefly here, a real, practical way one, single workflow file handles several, genuinely separate, real deployments.
This pattern keeps a real, growing CI setup genuinely maintainable, rather than several, separate, duplicated workflow files.

blocks.alt: One, real workflow file, running the same, genuine pipeline, per separate environment

blocks.content:
strategy:
  matrix:
    environment: [dev, staging, production]
8. A Real, Common Mistake
A static AWS key, stored as a real, long-lived GitHub secret, is a real, common mistake, especially before OIDC federation is genuinely understood and adopted.
This directly recreates the exact real risk already covered, a long-lived credential that remains genuinely valid indefinitely, if ever leaked.
The honest fix is exactly OIDC federation, already covered earlier in this topic, genuinely removing this real risk entirely.
This mistake is worth catching immediately in any real, new pipeline setup, before a static key is ever genuinely committed to a secret store.
